title: Sort the People
description:
# Sort the People

You are given two arrays of equal length:

* `names[i]` is the name of the `i`th person.
* `heights[i]` is the height of the `i`th person.

All heights are **distinct**. Return the names sorted by height from tallest to shortest.

Names are not guaranteed to be unique, so the height or original index must keep each person paired with the correct name.

## Example 1

**Input:** names = ["Mary","John","Emma"], heights = [180,165,170]
**Output:** ["Mary","Emma","John"]
**Explanation:** Mary is tallest, then Emma, then John.

## Example 2

**Input:** names = ["Alice","Bob","Bob"], heights = [155,185,150]
**Output:** ["Bob","Alice","Bob"]
**Explanation:** The first Bob has height `185`, while the second Bob has height `150`.

## Constraints

* `n == names.length == heights.length`
* `1 <= n <= 1000`
* `1 <= names[i].length <= 20`
* `1 <= heights[i] <= 100000`
* `names[i]` contains only lowercase and uppercase English letters.
* All values in `heights` are distinct.

solutions.name: Sort Indices By Height
solutions.description:
## Approach

Create an array of indices `0..n-1`. Sort those indices by the corresponding height in descending order, then read names in that sorted index order.

## Key Insight

Sorting indices keeps the original `names[i]` and `heights[i]` pairing intact. This matters because names can repeat, so sorting names directly would lose which height belongs to which person.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n log n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: TreeMap From Height To Name
solutions.description:
## Approach

Put each `(height, name)` pair into a `TreeMap` ordered by descending height. Since heights are unique, each height maps to exactly one person.

## Key Insight

The problem gives distinct heights, so height is a safe key even when names repeat. Reading the map values in key order directly gives tallest to shortest.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n log n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Max Heap By Height
solutions.description:
## Approach

Push every person into a priority queue ordered by height from largest to smallest. Polling the queue repeatedly produces names in the required order.

## Key Insight

A max heap models the repeated operation "take the tallest remaining person." Storing the original index in the heap keeps duplicate names separated.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n log n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Bounded Height Table Scan
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the constraint `1 <= heights[i] <= 100000`. Store `name` at `byHeight[height]`, then scan the table from height `100000` down to `1` and collect non-empty entries.

## Key Insight

When the value range is small enough, a direct-address table can replace a comparison sort. Distinct heights make each table slot hold at most one person.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n + H), where H = 100000
- Space Complexity: O(H)
